Aleutian Islands is outlined by Coats (1947,1956). Kanaton Ridge (KAN) forms the caldera rim of ancient Mount Kanaton, a broad shield volcano constructed, according to Coats, during late Tertiary and Quaternary time. However, a whole rock K-Ar date run on a sample taken a few feet above the top flow cored gave a date of only 0.18 f0-09 My. The section is composed of a sequence of nearly horizontal basalt and andesite flows, of which eight were sampled. The samples were taken from an eastward trending ridge just outside the ancient caldera rim, and about 45km south-east of Kanaga Volcano (51" 54' N, 182" 54' E). On the basis of pilot AF demagnetization tests (Fig. 2(a), and (b)), the samples were all demagnetized in peak fields of 380Oe. Palaecwecular variation of the geomagnetic field 319 The mean directions from Kanaton are well grouped with the exception of Flow 8 (Fig. 2(c) and (d)). Cores showing magnetically low dips and both normal and reversed directions are present in this flow. It was decided that these cores represent two flows, the one being normal with low dip and high scatter and the other being reversed with low dip but very small scatter (Table 1). This is consistent with relative core locations in the outcrop, though no field evidence for separate flows was noted.

these flows, it is presumed that they were extruded while the geomagnetic field was undergoing a reversal and therefore represent a period of unstable field behaviour (e.g. Creer & Ispir 1970); thus, they have been omitted from the statistical analysis. The remaining seven flows have vector directions and VGP's which are closely grouped (k = 136 and 58, respectively) about the axial dipole field direction and the geographic pole, (Table 1 and Fig. 2(c) and (d)). The distribution is approximately axially symmetric. A clear serial correlation from one flow to the next is evident, indicating that perhaps these seven flows were extruded fairly rapidly and do not represent the full spectrum of secular variation, generally considered to span about lo4 yr, A two-tier analysis (Watson & Irving 1957) was carried out on flows 1-7. The variance ratio proved significant at the 95 per cent level so that calculated values for k, and kp are given in Table 2. The number of flows is too small for a reliable measurement of PSV to be possible; nevertheless, we may take kp = 239 as being a minimum measure (maximum k) of PSV during the time of extrusion. It is deduced from the palaeomagnetism of these Basalts that some modifications should be made to their strati- graphy and these deductions have been substantiated by radiometric studies described in the following paper. on of flows of feldspathic basalt, frequently containing abundant olivine and sometimes associated with thick beds of breccias and tuffs. Groeber (1933) attributed the origin of these basaltic flows to eruptions following the second Andean tectonic phase during the Miocene. This age has been substantiated by the presence of Santa-Crucean fossils in tuffs contemporaneous with flows. Basalt I1 (Coyocholitense) is supposed to be of Upper Pliocene age, corres- ponding to effusions which followed the third Andean tectonic phase. In the zone outside the cordillera, this basalt forms extensive tablelands which are cut by the erosion of streams because it was later strongly uplifted. It is often possible to recognize the skeletal remains of the volcanoes from which these flows were extruded. Towards the end of the Pliocene, diastrophism produced a topography similar to the present one on which the products of a new effusive cycle accumulated in the Middle Pleistocene. Groeber (1933) named these flows Basalt I11 (Lower Chapuali- tense). They are highly eroded and generally exist singly, rarely forming successions of flows. The original volcanoes are well preserved. We can make some con- clusions about the secondary magnetization from blocking temperatures observed on the thermal decay curves (plots of intensity versus temperature). The blocking temperature of a single mag- netic grain is the temperature at which the magnetic relaxation time (proportional to exp (aV/T), where V is the grain volume, T is tem- perature, and a is a function of the magnetic properties of the particle [Nel, 1955]) is of the order of the duration of the experiment, say 10 minutes. The blocking temperature thus determines the time constant of the magnetiza- tion of any lower temperature, assuming that the other parameters are constant. This rela- tionship has been conveniently plotted by Chamalaun [1964]. If there are a large number of grains in a rock sample with similar blocking temperatures, the thermal decay curves will show an abrupt change in intensity over a narrow range around an average specimen blocking temperature. Of course, during a ther- mal demagnetization, the moments of some grains are randomized by each heating, for there is usually a continuous distribution in grain size (V). We can make some con- clusions about the secondary magnetization from blocking temperatures observed on the thermal decay curves (plots of intensity versus temperature). The blocking temperature of a single mag- netic grain is the temperature at which the magnetic relaxation time (proportional to exp (aV/T), where V is the grain volume, T is tem- perature, and a is a function of the magnetic properties of the particle [Nel, 1955]) is of the order of the duration of the experiment, say 10 minutes. The blocking temperature thus determines the time constant of the magnetiza- tion of any lower temperature, assuming that the other parameters are constant. This rela- tionship has been conveniently plotted by Chamalaun [1964]. If there are a large number of grains in a rock sample with similar blocking temperatures, the thermal decay curves will show an abrupt change in intensity over a narrow range around an average specimen blocking temperature. Of course, during a ther- mal demagnetization, the moments of some grains are randomized by each heating, for there is usually a continuous distribution in grain size (V). The evidence from the present study indicates that grain size is the most important factor, whereas the titano- maghemite content is of subordinate impor- tance. It should be emphasized that the two major rock types grade into one another, so that the boundary between the phases shown in Figure I is somewhat arbitrary. The chilled borders of the sill are basalt. The effect of baking on the country rock is evidenced by a zone of hornfels extending  few feet above and below the chilled borders. More complete petrologic dis- cussions are given by Roberts [1953] and Snavely and Wagner [1961]. The temperature of intrusion is a matter of conjecture. Polished sections of samples from the chilled borders show titanomagnetite grains that must have formed prior to emplace- ment. Since magnetite will not form above ap- proximately 1500øC, the temperature of intru- sion must have been below this value. Melting experiments by Tilley et al. [1963] indicate a liquidus temperature for the Skaergaard gab- broic magma of approximately 1230øC, and Winklet [1965] suggests 1200øC as the intru- sion temperature of the typical gabbroic magma. Differentiation by crystal settling and frac- tional crystallization followed the liquid in- trusion [Roberts, 1953]. The exceptional thick- ness of the intrusion and great depth of burial maintained the magma in a liquid s

ugh transfer of material and volatile constituents and the upward movement of the surface of crystallization [Jaeger, 1958]. At the time crystallization ceased, the granophyric diorite zone was very likely at a nearly uniform high temperature. The final pegmatitic phase had an involved crystallization history. Experiments by Tilley et al. [1963] show that crystallization of peg- matitc constituent minerals takes place over a range of 200 ø to 300øC. The intrasite coherence of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) directions indicates that the remanent mag- netization of the pegmatite phase was acquired after solidification. Curie temperatures meas- ured in this region are approximately 550øC, and the ferromagnetic minerals are interstitial to the other mineral grains in the pegmatite. This indicates that solidification of this facies must have been complete above the Curie tem- perature. The maximum development of the pegmatite is approximately 300 meters above the base of the sill, according to field observa- tions. These observations are confirmed by chemical analyses, which indicate a maximum silica content at this level (Parke Snavely, Jr., personal communication). INTRODUCTION The earth's magnetic field is subject to varia- tion over an extremely broad time spectrum, and its analysis is based largely on direct ob- servatory measurements [Hide and Roberts, 1961; Yukatake, 1962; McDonald and Watson, 1968]. These measurements date only to the sixteenth century [Bauer, 1895] and conse- quently provide no information about compo- nents of secular variation with longer periods. Palcomagnetic studies, although contributing greatly to the knowledge of earlier changes in the earth's field, suffer from the limitation that they yield ancient field directions known as a function of stratigraphy, but not generally as a function of time. A means of obtaining a con- tinuous time record of the magnetic field, first suggested by Jaeger and Green [1956], is the study of the palcomagnetic record of an in- trusive body. Moreover, as noted several decades ago by Fisk [1931], the secular variation (rate of change of the geomagnetic elements) is also anomalously low in this region. In previous reports [Doell and Cox, 1963, 1965a], we have presented data and tentative arguments suggesting that this 'window' in the nondipole field is a relatively permanent feature, having existed throughout most of the last, or Brunhes, polarity epoch. section_candidates.excerpt: rpentinization. The stablilly of mag- netization decreases with serpentinization, owing to the growth of larger magnetic grains. Thus, in highly serpentinized peridotires (serpentinites), most of the CRM is destroyed and the NRM becomes mainly viscous reinanent magnetization, rendering these rocks unsuitable for palcomagnetic work. On the other hand, in partially serpentinized peridotires, pyroxenites, and dunires, the CRM is highly stable and palcomagnetically reliable. A study of the stable directions of magnetization indicates that the Red Mountain ultramarie body was emplaced and serpentinized prior to the folding of the Franciscan formation. The stability of magneti- zation and removal of viscous components were verified by the results of a storage test and alternating-field demagnetization experiments, by the divergence of the mean directions of magnetization from that of the present field, and, most important, by the convergence of the directions after tilt correction. Palcomagnetic pole positions calculated from the mean directions suggest that the magnetic pole rapidly migrated southward into the Atlantic Ocean during late Mesozoic, possibly more than once, as proposed previously by Gromm and Gluskoter. INTRODUCTION The present study deals with the paleomagnetism of rock samples from the Indian Gondwana sediments, collected during a field trip in the winter season of 1966-1967. The Indian subcontinent is considered to have formed part of the Gondwana continents of the Southern Hemisphere, because of paleontological similarities. Paleomagnetic studies on the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Eocene plateau basalts of the Deccan traps (DEuTSCH et al., 1959) as well as on the Jurassic Rajmahal traps (CLEGG et al., 1958) and Sylhet traps (ATHAVALE et al., 1963) have demonstrated that during the Upper Mesozoic India was situated south of the equator. WENSINK Geological Institute, State University, Utrecht (The Netherlands') (Received July 2, 1968) (Resubmitted October 30, 1968) SUMMARY Oriented samples were collected for paleomagnetic research from red horizons of the Gondwana sediments at a few localities in central India. The specimens were subjected to both alternating-field and thermal demagnetization and were measured on astatic magnetometers. Usually a stable direction of magnetization was observed only after thermal treatment. The following results were obtained: (1) The Upper Permian Kamthi Beds reveal a mean direction of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp

of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp = 5.7 ° and dm = 7.3°); (3) The Upper Triassic Pachmarhi Beds have D = 117.2 °, I = +48.9 ° (pole position 10.15°N 49.9°W; dp = 4.0 ° and dm= 6.1 °). These results combined with earlier data indicate that the Indian sub- continent has made a sinistral rotation of about 90 ° during Upper Paleozoic through Mesozoic times, without a considerable meridional shift. INTRODUCTION The present study deals with the paleomagnetism of rock samples from the Indian Gondwana sediments, collected during a field trip in the winter season of 1966-1967. The Indian subcontinent is considered to have formed part of the Gondwana continents of the Southern Hemisphere, because of paleontological similarities. Paleomagnetic studies on the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Eocene plateau basalts of the Deccan traps (DEuTSCH et al., 1959) as well as on the Jurassic Rajmahal traps (CLEGG et al., 1958) and Sylhet traps (ATHAVALE et al., 1963) have demonstrated that during the Upper Mesozoic India was situated south of the equator. WENSINK Geological Institute, State University, Utrecht (The Netherlands') (Received July 2, 1968) (Resubmitted October 30, 1968) SUMMARY Oriented samples were collected for paleomagnetic research from red horizons of the Gondwana sediments at a few localities in central India. The specimens were subjected to both alternating-field and thermal demagnetization and were measured on astatic magnetometers. Usually a stable direction of magnetization was observed only after thermal treatment. The following results were obtained: (1) The Upper Permian Kamthi Beds reveal a mean direction of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp

of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp = 5.7 ° and dm = 7.3°); (3) The Upper Triassic Pachmarhi Beds have D = 117.2 °, I = +48.9 ° (pole position 10.15°N 49.9°W; dp = 4.0 ° and dm= 6.1 °). These results combined with earlier data indicate that the Indian sub- continent has made a sinistral rotation of about 90 ° during Upper Paleozoic through Mesozoic times, without a considerable meridional shift. INTRODUCTION The present study deals with the paleomagnetism of rock samples from the Indian Gondwana sediments, collected during a field trip in the winter season of 1966-1967. The Indian subcontinent is considered to have formed part of the Gondwana continents of the Southern Hemisphere, because of paleontological similarities. Paleomagnetic studies on the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Eocene plateau basalts of the Deccan traps (DEuTSCH et al., 1959) as well as on the Jurassic Rajmahal traps (CLEGG et al., 1958) and Sylhet traps (ATHAVALE et al., 1963) have demonstrated that during the Upper Mesozoic India was situated south of the equator. WENSINK Geological Institute, State University, Utrecht (The Netherlands') (Received July 2, 1968) (Resubmitted October 30, 1968) SUMMARY Oriented samples were collected for paleomagnetic research from red horizons of the Gondwana sediments at a few localities in central India. The specimens were subjected to both alternating-field and thermal demagnetization and were measured on astatic magnetometers. Usually a stable direction of magnetization was observed only after thermal treatment. The following results were obtained: (1) The Upper Permian Kamthi Beds reveal a mean direction of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp

of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp = 5.7 ° and dm = 7.3°); (3) The Upper Triassic Pachmarhi Beds have D = 117.2 °, I = +48.9 ° (pole position 10.15°N 49.9°W; dp = 4.0 ° and dm= 6.1 °). These results combined with earlier data indicate that the Indian sub- continent has made a sinistral rotation of about 90 ° during Upper Paleozoic through Mesozoic times, without a considerable meridional shift. INTRODUCTION The present study deals with the paleomagnetism of rock samples from the Indian Gondwana sediments, collected during a field trip in the winter season of 1966-1967. The Indian subcontinent is considered to have formed part of the Gondwana continents of the Southern Hemisphere, because of paleontological similarities. Paleomagnetic studies on the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Eocene plateau basalts of the Deccan traps (DEuTSCH et al., 1959) as well as on the Jurassic Rajmahal traps (CLEGG et al., 1958) and Sylhet traps (ATHAVALE et al., 1963) have demonstrated that during the Upper Mesozoic India was situated south of the equator. Palaeogeography, Palaeoelimatol., Palaeoecol., 5 (1968) 323-343 32

hey are overlain by Late Precambrian sediments and volcanics of the Cuddapah and Vindhyan Systems. Rocks of a Lower Paleozoic age are not found on the Indian subcontinent. The next stratigraphical unit is formed by a continental series which starts with glacial boulder beds and their associated peri-glacial beds of the Late Car- boniferous glaciation. From that time onwards sedimentation continues through the greater part of the Mesozoic until the Lower Cretaceous. All these deposits are classified in the Gondwana System. The rocks of the Gondwana System, which are chiefly composed of sand- stones and shales, are almost entirely deposited in fresh water. Intercalations of coal measures occur; they are mainly found in the lower part of the system. The subdivision of the Gondwana System into two subsystems is based on the content of plants: the Lower Gondwana System is characterized by the Glossopteris flora; the younger Upper Gondwana System can be distinguished from it by a cycadaceous Ptilophyllum flora. The transition between the Lower and the Upper Gondwana Systems takes place in the Upper Triassic. Apart from the subdivision into two separate systems advocated both by PASCOE (1959) and by KRISHNAN (1960), another subdivision is given by WADIA (1953) viz., into t

e Glossopteris flora; the younger Upper Gondwana System can be distinguished from it by a cycadaceous Ptilophyllum flora. The transition between the Lower and the Upper Gondwana Systems takes place in the Upper Triassic. Apart from the subdivision into two separate systems advocated both by PASCOE (1959) and by KRISHNAN (1960), another subdivision is given by WADIA (1953) viz., into three systems. Wadia distinguishes the Lower, the Middle, and the Upper Gondwana Systems. These coincide with the Upper Carboniferous-Permian, the Triassic, and the Jurassic together with the Lower Cretaceous respectively. The Gondwana sediments are deposited in a number of basins. The local stratigraphies which have been drawn up for the individual basins do not facilitate the establishment of a stratigraphy that is representative for the whole Gondwana System. The preservation of the Gondwana sediments is largely a result of faulting subsequent to the deposition of the beds concerned. A vast area of the western and central parts of the Indian peninsula is covered by a series of plateau basalts-the Deccan traps-which have a thickness of at least 1,500 m. It is bordered by crystalline massifs save only in the south-west where there is tectonic contact with the Permian to Mesozoic fill of the Hronov Graben. The south-east and north-west margins of the Depres­ sion are formed by the crystalline rocks of the Góry Orlickie, Góry By­ strzyckie and Kłodzko massifs, a

A Namurian C to lower Westphalian A age is generally accepted for the Biały Kamień Formation. The Biały Kamień Formation gradually passes upwards to the Zacier Formation. In north-eastern part of the Depression the age of the Żacler Formation (up to 900 m thick) is regarded as Westphalian A and B, while in the south-western part of the Depression it also includes Westphalian C. The lower part of the formation consists mainly of sandstones and silt­ stones with coal seams. In the upper part of the formation sandstones and conglomerates dominate. The south-east and north-west margins of the Depres­ sion are formed by the crystalline rocks of the Góry Orlickie, Góry By­ strzyckie and Kłodzko massifs, and the Karkonosze-Góry Izerskie massifs respectively. It is bordered by crystalline massifs save only in the south-west where there is tectonic contact with the Permian to Mesozoic fill of the Hronov Graben. The south-east and north-west margins of the Depres­ sion are formed by the crystalline rocks of the Góry Orlickie, Góry By­ strzyckie and Kłodzko massifs, and the Karkonosze-Góry Izerskie massifs respectively. The north-east flank is formed by the Caledonides of the Góry Kacza wskie and the gneiss of the Góry Sowie mountains (Figs. 1, 2). The Inner Sudetic Depression is a Variscan structure, accentuated by bordering faults which generally parallel the Elbe line and which were reactivated in younger geological times. Tertiary orogenic move­ ments resulted in a dominantly Saxonian type tectonic structure. Since the Visean, and possibly even within the Tournaisian, the De­ pression was an area of deposition in which accumulated locally derived, predominantly fresh-water sediments, throughout the Upper Carbonifero­ us to Permian into Lower Triassic (Bunter) times. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of three of the bands was significantly misaligned with the present Earth's field. Sixty-nine specimens were then subjected to detailed demag- netization in alternating fields to 795 peak Oe and temperatures to 670°C. The results demonstrated that the NRM of the four bands is dominated by a very stable component with blocking temperature in the 400-550°C range. A positive fold test indicates that this magnetization was acquired prior to the folding of the Mweelrea syncline in the Ordovieian or earliest Silurian. Stanton [12] dates the grits as Middle Ordovician, along with the underlying Glenummera Series. Origin of the magnetization The ignimbrites have been described [11, 12] as welded tuffs resulting from a nude ardente-type magma highly charged with gases. Dewey [ 11 ] ob- served magnetite concentrations around the margins of gas-explosion nuclei. Covering an area of some 200-300 km 2 without marked compositional variation, these tuffs appear to have been rapidly chilled, perhaps due to deposition in shallow water [12]. ent paleomagnetic data must be considered as a maximum estimate of the paleomagnetic field secular variation. It might be argued that the formation of the Monteregian Hills may have been an event of short duration, so that the above data cannot be used as a reliable gage of the secular varia- tion in Cretaceous time. It is pointed out, how- ever, that the group of intrusives has witnessed at least one earth's field reversal during its c.ooling, and, if it is correct to estimate with Cox and Dalrymple [1967] that this phenome- non spreads over about 5000 years, the Monte- regian Hills may have taken that long to cool through the Curie point of magnetite. In the perspective of the numerous Rb/Sr and K/Ar age determinations reported by Fairbairn et al. [1963] ,on the Monteregian Hills, it appears, however, that the group of intrusives may in fact have taken several million years to form. That the earth's field was apparently entirely dipolar in Cretaceous time is also suggested by the apparently reliable pole positions derived from other widely separated North American formations of this period. The high clustering of these poles about their center of gravity [Larochelie, 1968a] suggests that the 'wobble' of the dipole at that time was much less pro- nounced t

supports the view that the Oka and Mount Megantic intrusives are true extensions of the Monteregian Hills proper. Finally, the low angular standard deviation of the analyzed data suggests that in Cretaceous time the non-dipole component of the earth's magnetic field was less important relative to the dipole field than it is today. In this paper we will follow the usage of Smith and Bailey (1966) and use the informal terms, lower member and upper member. The lower member comprises Grigg's Otowi (an ash-flow unit) and the underlying Guaje Member (the associated air-fall unit), and the upper member constitutes the Tshirege Member, including the basal air-fall pumice. Thus, each of the lower and upper members consist of an ash-flow unit and its associated basal air-fall pumice. The lower member overlies a marked erosional unconformity that is de- veloped on the older volcanic rocks of the Jemez Mountains. The upper member, in turn, is separated from the lower member by a marked erosional disconformity and locally by bedded tuffs, glowing avalanche deposits, and volcanic sediments that related to the Cerro Toledo Rhyolite of the Toledo Caldera (PL 1). The internal stratigraphy of both members of

es permit correlation of units within each member with a high degree of confidence. The phenocryst mineralogy of the Bandelier Tuff is at first glance monotonously simple: major quartz, sanidine, and minor clinopyroxene, fayalite, and oxides. However, preliminary studies (Smith and Bailey, 1966) show that in the upper member, and prob- ably also in the lower member, systematic chemical and mineralogical changes on January 18, 2014memoirs.gsapubs.orgDownloaded from 216 STUDIES IN VOLCANOLOGY are recorded in pumices from successively emplaced flows. In the upper mem- ber, the phenocryst content changes from about 5 percent in the basal air-fall pumice and lower ash flows to more than 30 percent in upper units. In the uppermost unit, anorthoclase and hypersthene take the place of sanidine and fayalite, and there is a marked decrease in quartz content. This upper anortho- clase unit is unique in the Jemez Mountains and is critical to the correlation of the Bandelier Tuff inside and outside the Valles Caldera. It is this unit that dominates the outcrop on the structural dome within the caldera, whereas only a few remnants have survived erosion outside the caldera. Intracaldera Rhyolites The rhyolites within the Valles Caldera may be conveniently divided into three group

ggests a temporal succession of the principal domes from Cerro del Medio westward to San Antonio Mountain, and, as will be discussed later in this paper, the K-Ar and paleomagnetic studies tend to confirm this general succession. Warm Springs dome, a small endogenous rhyolite dome that is now being exhumed from young lake beds and alluvium may belong to this subgroup, but its stratigraphic relationship with the other units is not cer- tainly known. The youngest rhyolite units in the Valles Caldera are the ash flows of Battleship Rock and the overlying obsidian flow of Banco Bonito, both of which apparently issued from the same vent. Petrographically, the rhyolites of Cerro del Medio are almost without phenocrysts, but an occasional small sanidine crystal may be seen. The other late rhyolite units, discussed here, contain phenocrysts of quartz, sanidine, biotite, and oxides, and show a general increase in femic minerals and total phenocryst content westward from Cerro del Medio. Hornblende and plagio- clase are common in the youngest, westernmost units (San Antonio Moun- tain, Battleship Rock, and Banco Bonito). Briefly, the only practical criterion is to ascertain that the primary stable component of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) has been clearly identified and measured. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: alifornia Paleomagnetic and potassium-argon studies support geologic evidence that the lower member of the Bandelier Tuff was deposited 1.4 m.y. ago. The upper member erupted about 1.0 m.y. ago and was followed by caldera collapse which formed the 12- to 14-mile diameter Valles Caldera. Post- caldera activity which resulted in the eruption of rhyolite domes and pyro- clastic material, has occurred at about 0.9, 0.7, 0.5, and 0.4 m.y. ago, with later undated eruptions that were estimated at about 0.1 m.y. ago. These data from the Valles Caldera are the basis for the previously pub- lished age revision of the Brunhes-Matuyama geomagnetic polarity epoch boundary from 1.0 to 0.7 m.y. ago, and they were used to define the Jaramillo normal polarity event at about 0.9 m.y. ago (Doell and Dalrymple, 1966). Younger Volcanic Series Lavas of the Younger Volcanic Series flooded the much eroded stumps of the old volcano to form an extensive intramontane plain, which slopes away from a central ridge. Two major periods of eruption are recognized, thought to have been separated by a relatively short period of quiescence. The Early Lavas are now only exposed in southwest Mauritius (Fig. 2), but may well extend under the Late Lavas (Simpson, 1951). These Early Lavas are mas- sive to somewhat vesicular alkali olivine basalts, usually 3 to 10 m thick. Petrographically and chemically they form a rather uniform series and are nepheline normative (Walker and Nicolaysen, 1954). The Late Lavas cover the remainder of the island between the older massifs and were erupted from a chain of vents extending in a line striking north-northeast through Curepipe in the center of the isknd. The surface of the Late Lavas has been little modified by erosion, although a number of gorges have been cut by consequent streams. As recognized by all workers, the Late Lavas must be very young geologically. The lavas generally are thin (1 to 8 m) and highly vesicular, suggesting a rather volatile magma. They are entirely basal

The lavas generally are thin (1 to 8 m) and highly vesicular, suggesting a rather volatile magma. They are entirely basaltic and contain abundant olivine phenocrysts. Many of the lavas are relatively coarse grained, doleritic basalts with a subophitic or ophitic texture. Compositionally the Late Lavas show little variation and are nepheline normative; they are characterized by remarkably low potassium contents for alkali olivine basalts (Walker and Nicolaysen, 1954). Potassium was measured by flame photometry (Cooper, 1963), and the isotope dilution method was used for determining argon. A Reynolds-type mass spectrometer in the static mode of opera- tion was employed to measure the isotopic ratios of the argon. Sample MU 139 has a slightly altered appearance in thin section, but apart from alteration of olivine to iddingsite, MU 140 is fresh; some loss of radiogenic argon from MU 139 may have occurred. The overlying basalt contains abun- dant large crystals of olivine, clinopyroxene and plagioclase, some of which occur in aggre- gates and are possibly xenolithic. Whole rock analyses on two samples (MU 141, MU 142) give K-Ar dates that also disagree by more than the expected errors, but the dates are similar to that found for MU 140. A much older date of 10.1 ± 1.6 m.y. was found for large plagioclase crystals separated from MU 142, reinforcing the view that these crystals may be xenolithic. Alternatively, the plagioclase may carry excess radiogenic argon (compare with Damon and others, 1967). The terms magnetically "hard" and "soft" are used here to describe the amount of N.R.M. intensity associated with low coercivities. A magnetically soft sample loses its intensity of magnetization relatively rapidly during a.f. demagnetization and is therefore potentially more unstable than a magnetically hard rock. Profound erosion subse- quently destroyed much of the volcano, leaving only peripheral steep-sided massifs. steep-sided massifs. Lavas of the Younger Volcanic Series were erupted from about 3.5 m.y. ago until less than 0.2 m.y. ago, flood- ing the denuded stumps of the shield volcano. This activity was intermittent and a hiatus is recog- nized from about 2 to 0.7 m.y. ago, which we have taken as the break between the erupt-on of the Early and Late Lavas of the Younger Volcanic Series. The mean directions of magnetization of the three groups of lavas are not significantly different from one another and are close to an axial dipole direction. The combined paleomagnetic and dating studies on the lavas also yield further information on the geomagnetic polarity time scale; 16 results on rocks with ages lying between 3.5 and 0.17 m.y. are consistent with the established scale for this period of geological time. Of particular significance are results that confirm the Mammoth reversed event at 3.0 m.y. ago, and the age of the boundary between the Gauss normal and Gilbert reversed polarity epochs at 3.35 m.y. Nineteen results were obtained on rocks whose ages are between 4.6 and 7.9 m.y., and these data generally are consistent with the polarity time scale based upon extrapolations from the sea-floor spreading hypothesis. Introduction A considerable number of paleomagnetic studies of North American Precambrian rock units have been reported in the literature. How- ever, the geological age of most of the units studied is presently known only within wide limits. The construction of a North American Precambrian polar wandering curve will require many more paleomagnetic results from rock units that have been radiometrically dated. In the case of igneous rocks, units should be chosen for which the radiometric 'dates' are thought to be approximations to the geological 'age', i.e., rocks for which the post-crystallization thermal history has been simple. The Croker Island Complex, exposed on several islands in the North Channel of Lake Huron, appears to satisfy the above requirement. The age of the formations investigated varies from Ordovician to Eocene. Apart from geologic studies the Natural Remanent Magnetizations (N.R.M.) were analyzed with the aid of a.c. magnetic field and thermal demagnetization techniques. In the case of three folded formations the characteristic remanent magnetizations could be proved to be acquired before the subsequent folding took place. These formations are the Upper Silurian Almaden volcanics, the Upper Carboniferous-Lower Permian Bucaco Formation of Portugal and the Eocene basalts of the Lisbon region. All three other Upper Carboniferous- Lower Permian sample groups of Spain yield similar directions of magnet- ization. The natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.) of all samples was further analyzed by progressive demagnetization with a.c. magnetic fields up to 3,000 Oe (peak value). For an extensive description of the methods of measurement and the analysis of the N.R.M. with the aid of a-c. magnetic field demag~~etization the reader is referred to As and Zijderveld (1958), As (1960?, Van Everdingen (1960) and Zijderveld (1967a). Furthermore, several samples of each group were subjected to thermal demagnetization. For this treatment cores were drilled (diameter 25 mm, height 22 mm) from the hand samples oriented in the paraffin cubes. The demagnetization was carried out stepwise, the samples being heated and cooled again to room temperature in a furnace placed in a zero ambient field. The directions and intensities of the samples, being remeasured after each step, yielded extra information besides the a.c. magnetic field demagnetization, for instance on blocking temperatures and constitution of the N.R.M. For an extensive description of the furnace, I refer to Mulder and Zijderveld (in preparation). The directions of magnetization of the well-dated Upper Silurian Almaden volcanics (10 samples, 2 sites, 2 flows) have been analyzed with the aid of a.c. magnetic field demagnetizations. One of the two components, which were present in all samplds, had a direction parallel to the present-day geomagnetic field and is likely to be secondary. The difference in attitude of the two flows permits the application of the unfolding test and proves the other component to be pre-tectonic. The Atienza andesites have been collected at six sites from at least four petrographically different units (Van der Voo, 1967). The 33 samples yielded after elimination of the small secondary component very consistent “characteristic” directions. We adopt here the term “characteristic magnetization” for this component, because conclusive proof of the primary character of the residual component revealed by progressive demagnetization is lacking (no unfolding test). the Spanish Meseta, the redbeds of Alcazar de San Juan (Table I, no.20) were the only Triassic rocks to yield a characteristic direction of magnetization. Other investigations (Table I, no.lP18) revealed only (secondary) present-day geomagnetic field directions. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. It is, therefore, not surprising to observe some scattering of the Spanish results (Fig.33). Stable (extra-Alpine) Europe

It has intruded into Jurassic and Cretaceous sediments, which have been distorted and now form a dome- structure around the intrusive body. The natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.) of all samples was further analyzed by progressive demagnetization with a.c. magnetic fields up to 3,000 Oe (peak value). For an extensive description of the methods of measurement and the analysis of the N.R.M. with the aid of a-c. magnetic field demag~~etization the reader is referred to As and Zijderveld (1958), As (1960?, Van Everdingen (1960) and Zijderveld (1967a). Furthermore, several samples of each group were subjected to thermal demagnetization. For this treatment cores were drilled (diameter 25 mm, height 22 mm) from the hand samples oriented in the paraffin cubes. The demagnetization was carried out stepwise, the samples being heated and cooled again to room temperature in a furnace placed in a zero ambient field. The directions and intensities of the samples, being remeasured after each step, yielded extra information besides the a.c. magnetic field demagnetization, for instance on blocking temperatures and constitution of the N.R.M. For an extensive description of the furnace, I refer to Mulder and Zijderveld (in preparation). the Spanish Meseta, the redbeds of Alcazar de San Juan (Table I, no.20) were the only Triassic rocks to yield a characteristic direction of magnetization. Other investigations (Table I, no.lP18) revealed only (secondary) present-day geomagnetic field directions. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. the Spanish Meseta, the redbeds of Alcazar de San Juan (Table I, no.20) were the only Triassic rocks to yield a characteristic direction of magnetization. Other investigations (Table I, no.lP18) revealed only (secondary) present-day geomagnetic field directions. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. The natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.) of all samples was further analyzed by progressive demagnetization with a.c. magnetic fields up to 3,000 Oe (peak value). For an extensive description of the methods of measurement and the analysis of the N.R.M. with the aid of a-c. magnetic field demag~~etization the reader is referred to As and Zijderveld (1958), As (1960?, Van Everdingen (1960) and Zijderveld (1967a). Furthermore, several samples of each group were subjected to thermal demagnetization. For this treatment cores were drilled (diameter 25 mm, height 22 mm) from the hand samples oriented in the paraffin cubes. The demagnetization was carried out stepwise, the samples being heated and cooled again to room temperature in a furnace placed in a zero ambient field. the Spanish Meseta, the redbeds of Alcazar de San Juan (Table I, no.20) were the only Triassic rocks to yield a characteristic direction of magnetization. Other investigations (Table I, no.lP18) revealed only (secondary) present-day geomagnetic field directions. In the Spanish Pyrenees PermyTriassic redbeds have been inves- tigated in three areas (Table I, no.10,12,19). Their age may range between Late Carboniferous and Late Triassic, with a hiatus somewhere in the Permian (H. Visscher, personal communication, 1969). Paleomagnetically, however, there is an indication for a Triassic, perhaps an uppermost Permian age. A long period of reversed polarity, the so-called Kiaman Interval, is assumed to last till at least the end of the Middle Permian (Irving and Parry, 1963; McMahon and Strangway, 1968). In the redbeds of Garralda and the Sierra de1 Cadi mixed polarities occur. The volcanic rocks of the Huesca province (Table I, no.11,13) are contemporaneous with the HueSca redbeds as Schwarz (1962) demonstrated. Apart from the uncertainties about the age relationships, it is unknown to what extent the Alpine orogeny might have influenced the Pyrenean directions. The Late Mesozoic and’Early Tertiary periods might give evidence for the time-span of the postulated geotectonic move- ments. Ordovician and Silurian Previous investigations In an earlier presentation of part of this study (Van der Voo, 1967) I described the paleomagnetism of two sample groups of volcanics from Almad6n and Atienza (Table I, no.2,3). The directions of magnetization of the well-dated Upper Silurian Almaden volcanics (10 samples, 2 sites, 2 flows) have been analyzed with the aid of a.c. magnetic field demagnetizations. One of the two components, which were present in all samplds, had a direction parallel to the present-day geomagnetic field and is likely to be secondary. The difference in attitude of the two flows permits the application of the unfolding test and proves the other component to be pre-tectonic. The Atienza andesites have been collected at six sites from at least four petrographically different units (Van der Voo, 1967). The 33 samples yielded after elimination of the small secondary component very consistent “characteristic” directions.
